title: MS Excel (Formulas & Functions)
subtitle: Cells, references, formulas, VLOOKUP, charts, sort/filter and pivot tables - the most-tested MS Office topic

readingSections.title: Cells, Ranges & References (Relative, Absolute, Mixed)
readingSections.quickSummary: Cell = column letter + row number (A1). Range = two cells with a colon (A1:B10). References are Relative (no $) or Absolute ($A$1) or Mixed ($A1 or A$1). F4 toggles.
content: A CELL in Excel is identified by its CELL ADDRESS: a column letter (A, B, C, ... Z, AA, AB, ... XFD) and a row number (1, 2, 3, ... 1048576). A1 is the top-left cell. The active cell is the one currently selected (the Name Box shows its address).

A RANGE is a rectangular block of cells, written as two addresses separated by a colon. A1:B10 means column A-B, rows 1-10 = 20 cells. A1:A1 is a single cell. You can also use whole-column references like A:A (all 1,048,576 cells in column A) or whole-row references like 5:5.

A WORKSHEET in modern Excel (2007+) has 1,048,576 rows and 16,384 columns. That gives 17.2 billion cells per sheet. Columns end at XFD (the 16,384th column letter). The 2^20 and 2^14 binary boundaries explain the magic numbers. Press Ctrl+End to jump to the last used cell.

There are three kinds of CELL REFERENCES. RELATIVE (A1) - the default - shifts when you copy a formula to another cell. ABSOLUTE ($A$1) - stays locked when you copy. MIXED ($A1 or A$1) - locks the column OR the row but not both. The $ sign in front of the column letter locks the column; in front of the row number locks the row.

F4 is the magic shortcut. While editing a formula, click a cell reference and press F4 to cycle through the four states: A1 -> $A$1 -> A$1 -> $A1 -> A1. F4 only works in formula edit mode (start with =, then click a cell, then press F4).

subsections.title: When to use which reference
subsections.content: Use RELATIVE (A1) when you want the formula to repeat the same logic across a range - e.g. =A1*2 copied down column B will compute each row's double. Use ABSOLUTE ($A$1) when you want a fixed value - e.g. a tax rate in $A$1 applied to every cell in a column =B1*$A$1. Use MIXED ($A1) when you want a fixed column but sliding row (rare).

subsections.title: Cell references across sheets
subsections.content: To reference a cell in another sheet of the same workbook, use =SheetName!CellAddress. Example: =Sheet2!A1. If the sheet name has a space, wrap in single quotes: ='Sales 2024'!B5. To reference another workbook entirely: ='[Budget.xlsx]Sheet1'!A1.

quickRevision: Cell address = column letter + row number (e.g. A1, B5, XFD1048576).
Range = A1:B10 (rectangle), A:A (whole column), 5:5 (whole row).
Per sheet: 1,048,576 rows x 16,384 columns (XFD).
Reference types: Relative A1, Absolute $A$1, Mixed $A1 / A$1.
tricks: If the option lists 'A1' as an absolute reference -> wrong (A1 is relative).
F4 only works inside a formula (=A1 then F4). It does NOT toggle a reference when the cell is just selected.
Whole-column reference A:A is NOT the same as A1:A1048576 - A:A includes rows beyond your data as you add it.
Last column = XFD (16,384th). The exam often asks this.
patterns: 'Maximum rows in an Excel worksheet?' -> 1,048,576.
'Maximum columns in an Excel worksheet?' -> 16,384 (XFD).
'Shortcut to toggle reference types?' -> F4 (in formula edit mode).
'Difference between A1 and $A$1?' -> A1 relative (shifts on copy), $A$1 absolute (locked).

readingSections.title: Core Functions: SUM, AVERAGE, IF, COUNTIF, VLOOKUP
readingSections.quickSummary: SUM / AVERAGE / COUNT / MIN / MAX are the basic stats. IF / COUNTIF / SUMIF add logic. VLOOKUP / HLOOKUP / INDEX-MATCH are lookups. All start with = and the function name in caps.
content: Every formula in Excel starts with =. The function name follows, then arguments in parentheses. =SUM(A1:A10) adds 10 cells. =AVERAGE(B1:B5) gives the mean. =COUNT(A1:A100) counts cells that contain NUMBERS only - text-containing cells are skipped.

Statistical family: SUM (add), AVERAGE (mean), MIN (smallest), MAX (largest), COUNT (count numbers), COUNTA (count non-empty cells, including text), COUNTBLANK (count empty cells), MEDIAN (middle value), MODE (most frequent), STDEV (standard deviation).

Logical family: IF(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false) - the workhorse. =IF(A1>=50, 'Pass', 'Fail'). AND, OR, NOT combine conditions. IFERROR(value, fallback) replaces an error with a friendly message - =IFERROR(VLOOKUP(...), 'Not found').

Conditional aggregates: COUNTIF(range, criteria) counts cells matching a single criterion. SUMIF(range, criteria, sum_range) sums cells matching a criterion. AVERAGEIF does the average. Examples: =COUNTIF(A:A, 'Delhi') counts all rows whose column A says 'Delhi'. =SUMIF(B:B, '>100', C:C) sums column C where column B > 100.

Lookup family: VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, col_index, FALSE) finds a value in the FIRST column of a table and returns a value from a column to the right. FALSE means exact match (use this in exams). HLOOKUP is the horizontal version - looks in the first ROW and returns a value from a row below. INDEX-MATCH is the more flexible combo: MATCH finds the position, INDEX returns the value at that position. INDEX-MATCH can look LEFT (VLOOKUP cannot).

subsections.title: VLOOKUP trap - exact vs approximate
subsections.content: VLOOKUP's 4th argument (range_lookup) is FALSE for EXACT match and TRUE (or omitted) for APPROXIMATE match. The exam's most common trap: 'What does FALSE mean in VLOOKUP?' -> Exact match. 'What if you omit it?' -> Approximate match (TRUE). Approximate match REQUIRES the first column to be sorted ascending - otherwise it returns wrong answers. Always use FALSE unless you have a sorted lookup table.

subsections.title: COUNTIF vs COUNTIFS
subsections.content: COUNTIF takes ONE criterion. COUNTIFS takes MULTIPLE criteria (all must match). Example: =COUNTIFS(A:A, 'Delhi', B:B, '>1000') counts rows where column A is Delhi AND column B > 1000. Same for SUMIFS, AVERAGEIFS - add the 'S' to get the multi-criteria version.

quickRevision: All formulas start with = and the function name in uppercase (Excel auto-capitalises).
Statistical: SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, COUNTA, MAX, MIN, MEDIAN.
Logical: IF, AND, OR, NOT, IFERROR.
Conditional: COUNTIF, SUMIF, AVERAGEIF (one criterion); COUNTIFS, SUMIFS, AVERAGEIFS (multiple).
Lookup: VLOOKUP (vertical), HLOOKUP (horizontal), INDEX-MATCH (most flexible).
VLOOKUP's last arg: FALSE = exact, TRUE/omitted = approximate.
tricks: COUNT counts numbers only; COUNTA counts anything non-empty (text included).
VLOOKUP only looks RIGHT - if you need to look LEFT, use INDEX-MATCH.
VLOOKUP's column_index is the number of the column IN the table, not the worksheet.
=VLOOKUP(A2, range, 3, FALSE) returns the 3rd column of the table.
patterns: 'Function to look up a value in the first column?' -> VLOOKUP.
'Function to look up a value in the first row?' -> HLOOKUP.
'Function to count cells meeting a condition?' -> COUNTIF.
'Function to sum cells meeting a condition?' -> SUMIF.
'What does FALSE in VLOOKUP mean?' -> Exact match.

readingSections.title: Worksheets, Workbooks & Navigation Shortcuts
readingSections.quickSummary: A workbook is a file (.xlsx). A workbook contains one or more worksheets (the tabs at the bottom). A worksheet has 1,048,576 rows x 16,384 columns. Ctrl+Page Up/Down switches tabs; Ctrl+Home goes to A1.
content: An Excel FILE is a WORKBOOK. The default file extension is .xlsx (since Excel 2007, replacing .xls). A workbook contains one or more WORKSHEETS - the tabs you see at the bottom of the window (Sheet1, Sheet2, ...). By default, a new workbook has 1 worksheet (or 3 in some older versions).

The CELL is the smallest unit. A row of cells is a RECORD; a column of cells is a FIELD. The column letter + row number is the cell address. The active cell is the highlighted one; its address appears in the NAME BOX on the left of the formula bar.

Three navigation shortcuts every exam asks about: Ctrl+Home jumps to cell A1. Ctrl+End jumps to the LAST USED cell in the worksheet (the bottom-right corner of your data). Ctrl+G (or F5) opens the Go-To dialog - jump to a specific cell address, named range, or comment.

Tab navigation: Ctrl+Page Down moves to the NEXT worksheet tab. Ctrl+Page Up moves to the PREVIOUS. Right-click the tab arrows at the bottom-left for a tab list. To create a new sheet, click the + next to the last tab, or press Shift+F11. To rename, double-click the tab name.

The Name Box (left of the formula bar) lets you type a cell address and press Enter to jump there - e.g. type 'Z500' to jump straight to Z500. You can also type a named range there. The formula bar shows the formula in the active cell; the cell shows the result.

subsections.title: Workbook protection
subsections.content: File > Info > Protect Workbook lets you lock the structure (preventing add/delete/rename/tab-reorder) with a password. Review > Protect Sheet protects individual cells - by default ALL cells are locked, but the protection does nothing until you enable it via Review > Protect Sheet. The trick: lock formatting or only specific ranges for editing.

subsections.title: Freeze panes
subsections.content: View > Freeze Panes keeps the top row, left column, or both visible while you scroll. Freeze Top Row (Alt+W, F, R) keeps row 1. Freeze First Column (Alt+W, F, C) keeps column A. To freeze both, click a cell in B2 and select Freeze Panes.

quickRevision: Workbook = .xlsx file. Worksheet = tab at the bottom of a workbook.
New workbook has 1 worksheet by default (Excel 2013+).
Active cell's address shows in the Name Box.
Ctrl+Home -> A1. Ctrl+End -> last used cell. F5 / Ctrl+G -> Go To.
Ctrl+Page Down / Page Up -> next / previous tab.
Shift+F11 -> new worksheet. F2 -> edit active cell.
tricks: Ctrl+End goes to the last USED cell - if you have stray formatting, this can land you far below your real data. Use Ctrl+End after pressing Ctrl+Home to spot the gap.
If the question lists 'Ctrl+End' as 'go to last cell of the document' -> right. 'last cell with data' is closer to right but technically 'last used'.
Newer Excel (Office 365) has 1 sheet by default; older had 3. The exam usually goes with 1 unless a specific version is mentioned.
patterns: 'Shortcut to go to A1?' -> Ctrl+Home.
'Shortcut to jump to the last used cell?' -> Ctrl+End.
'Shortcut to switch to the next worksheet?' -> Ctrl+Page Down.
'Shortcut to open Go To dialog?' -> F5 (or Ctrl+G).

readingSections.title: Cell Formatting, Number Formats & Charts
readingSections.quickSummary: Formatting = making data look right (number formats, alignment, borders, colours). Charts = Insert tab > Chart - pick from Column, Bar, Line, Pie, Scatter. Each chart has a data range and a chart type.
content: NUMBER FORMATS tell Excel how to DISPLAY a number without changing the value. General is the default. Currency adds a currency symbol ($, Rs, €). Percentage multiplies by 100 and adds %. Date / Time displays as a date or time. Custom lets you type your own format code (e.g. #,##0.00 for thousands with 2 decimal places).

Where to apply formatting: Home tab > Number group > dropdown (or Ctrl+1 for the full Format Cells dialog). Common exam fact: a cell with value 0.85 formatted as Percentage shows as 85%. The value stays 0.85 in the formula bar.

Charts (Insert tab > Chart) are visual representations of data. Common types: COLUMN (vertical bars, default), BAR (horizontal bars), LINE (trends), PIE (proportions of a whole), SCATTER (X-Y relationships), AREA (stacked line). To create a chart, select the data first (or any cell in the data), then Insert > Chart > pick a type.

Every chart has these key pieces: DATA RANGE (the cells being plotted), CHART TYPE (column, bar, line, etc.), AXES (X = categories, Y = values), LEGEND (colour key), TITLE, DATA LABELS (numbers on the bars/points). Right-click any of these in an existing chart to edit them.

FORMATTING tricks: Merge & Center (Home > Merge & Center) joins cells and centres the text. Wrap Text (Home > Wrap Text) wraps long text inside a cell. Borders (Home > Borders dropdown) add cell borders. Conditional Formatting (Home > Conditional Formatting) auto-formats cells based on rules - e.g. highlight all values > 100 in red.

subsections.title: Number format codes you'll see in MCQs
subsections.content: 0 = digit placeholder (shows digit or 0 if missing). # = digit placeholder (shows nothing if missing). , = thousand separator. . = decimal point. % = percent. $ = currency. @ = text placeholder. So #,##0.00 shows a number with commas and 2 decimal places (1234.5 -> 1,234.50). 0% on the value 0.85 shows 85%.

subsections.title: Chart shortcut
subsections.content: Press F11 with a cell selected to instantly create a default column chart on a new sheet ('Chart1'). Alt+F1 creates the chart on the same sheet. These are quick ways to preview data; you'll then edit the chart type and formatting.

quickRevision: Number format = how a value is displayed, not the value itself.
Currency, Percentage, Date, Time, Custom - the main number format types.
Ctrl+1 opens the Format Cells dialog with every format option.
Charts: Column, Bar, Line, Pie, Scatter, Area (and 3D versions).
F11 = instant default column chart on a new sheet. Alt+F1 = same chart on the current sheet.
tricks: If the question lists '0.85 displays as 0.85%' -> wrong. Formatted as Percentage, 0.85 displays as 85%.
F11 works only when a cell is selected; it ignores the selected range and uses the contiguous data.
Conditional Formatting > Highlight Cells Rules > Greater Than is a 2-click rule - the exam tests this often.
patterns: 'Shortcut to open the Format Cells dialog?' -> Ctrl+1.
'Shortcut to create a default chart on a new sheet?' -> F11.
'Cell value 0.85 formatted as Percentage displays as:' -> 85%.
'Which chart for showing trends over time?' -> Line chart.

readingSections.title: Data Tools: Sort, Filter, Find & Replace, Remove Duplicates
readingSections.quickSummary: Sort arranges rows by a column. Filter hides rows that don't match. Find/Replace (Ctrl+F / Ctrl+H) searches text. Remove Duplicates drops repeated rows. Data tab owns all of these.
content: SORT arranges rows by the values in one or more columns. Data > Sort opens a dialog with 'My data has headers' (always tick this if your data has a header row). Pick a column from the 'Sort by' dropdown, choose A-Z or Z-A, then click OK. Multi-level sort (Sort by > Then by) lets you sort by City, then by Name, etc.

FILTER hides rows that don't match a criterion, so you see only the data you care about. Data > Filter adds dropdown arrows to every header. Click the arrow on the column you want to filter, untick the values you want to hide, or use Number/Text Filters for conditions like 'greater than 100' or 'begins with D'. Clear the filter via Data > Clear.
ADVANCED FILTER (Data > Advanced) lets you filter to a DIFFERENT range or extract a unique list. Useful when the basic filter dropdown is too restrictive.

FIND & REPLACE: Ctrl+F opens Find. Ctrl+H opens Find and Replace. Replace All replaces every occurrence in one click. Use Options for case-sensitive or whole-word matching. Note: Ctrl+H is the same shortcut as in MS Word - find/replace works the same way across the Office apps.

REMOVE DUPLICATES (Data > Remove Duplicates) deletes rows whose values are identical in the selected columns. It does NOT highlight - it deletes. The exam asks for the difference between 'highlight duplicates' (Conditional Formatting > Highlight Duplicates) and 'remove duplicates' (permanently delete).

TEXT TO COLUMNS (Data > Text to Columns) splits a single column of data into multiple columns - e.g. 'Aarav Sharma' into first-name and last-name columns. It uses Delimiter (comma, tab, semicolon) or Fixed Width as the split rule.

subsections.title: Sort gotcha: the 'Expand the selection' choice
subsections.content: When you sort a single column without first selecting the whole data range, Excel asks 'Do you want to expand the selection to include adjacent data?'. Always click 'Expand' - otherwise only the sorted column moves and the data in other columns stays put, scrambling your rows.

subsections.title: AutoFilter vs Advanced Filter
subsections.content: AutoFilter (Data > Filter) is the dropdown-based filter - good for one criterion or a few checkboxes. Advanced Filter (Data > Advanced) lets you build complex AND/OR conditions in a criteria range (a small block of cells that lists the rules) and even copy the filtered output to a different location. AutoFilter is what the exam tests most often.

quickRevision: Data tab: Sort, Filter, Text to Columns, Remove Duplicates, Validation, Subtotal.
Sort: A-Z / Z-A; multi-level via 'Then by'. Always tick 'My data has headers'.
Filter: Data > Filter adds dropdowns to headers. Clear via Data > Clear.
Find Ctrl+F, Replace Ctrl+H (same as Word).
Remove Duplicates permanently deletes; Conditional Formatting only highlights.
tricks: If the question says 'highlight duplicates' -> Conditional Formatting > Highlight Cells Rules > Duplicate Values.
If the question says 'remove duplicates' -> Data > Remove Duplicates (DESTRUCTIVE).
When sorting, the 'Expand the selection' prompt is THE exam trap. Always expand.
patterns: 'Tab for Sort and Filter?' -> Data.
'Shortcut for Find?' -> Ctrl+F.
'Shortcut for Find and Replace?' -> Ctrl+H.
'To split a column into multiple columns?' -> Data > Text to Columns.

readingSections.title: Pivot Tables & Subtotals
readingSections.quickSummary: Pivot Table = summarise large data by category. Insert > PivotTable. Drag fields to Rows, Columns, Values, Filters. Subtotal = automatic =SUM() below each group when you Sort data and use Data > Subtotal.
content: A PIVOT TABLE is a summarisation tool. It takes a large flat list (e.g. one row per sale) and groups it by categories (e.g. total sales per region per product), then sums / counts / averages the numbers. You don't write a single formula - you drag fields around.

To create one: click any cell in your data, Insert > PivotTable (or Alt+N, V). Excel auto-detects the data range. The PivotTable Fields pane has four boxes: ROWS (categories down the side), COLUMNS (categories across the top), VALUES (the numbers to aggregate), FILTERS (a field that filters the whole table).

Example: sales data with columns Region, Product, Sales. Drag Region to Rows, Product to Columns, Sales to Values. You get a grid: one row per region, one column per product, the cells = sum of sales. Drag Region to Filters and you can pick a single region to view.

VALUE FIELD SETTINGS let you change how the value is aggregated - Sum, Count, Average, Max, Min, Product. Right-click any value in the pivot and choose 'Value Field Settings'. The exam's classic: 'How do I change Sum to Count in a Pivot Table?' -> Right-click > Value Field Settings > Count.

SUBTOTAL (a different feature) automatically inserts =SUBTOTAL() formulas below each group when your data is sorted by the same column. Data > Subtotal. It is the legacy way to do what Pivot Tables now do better. The formula =SUBTOTAL(function_num, range) lets you manually create subtotals that ignore other SUBTOTAL formulas (so nested subtotals don't double-count).

subsections.title: PivotTable shortcuts
subsections.content: Alt+N, V - Insert PivotTable dialog. Alt+Down Arrow - open the field dropdown. Right-click any value cell to refresh, change Value Field Settings, or show details (which double-clicks through to the underlying rows). Ctrl+Alt+F5 - refresh the pivot table when the source data changes.

subsections.title: PivotTable vs Subtotal - when to use which
subsections.content: Use PIVOT TABLE when: your data has many columns and you want to slice by any combination; you want to drag fields around to explore; you want to filter at the top. Use SUBTOTAL when: you want a one-shot summary in place; the data is sorted; you want =SUBTOTAL() formulas visible in cells (some people prefer the transparency). For the exam, the answer to 'summarise a large dataset quickly' is almost always Pivot Table.

quickRevision: Pivot Table = drag-and-drop summarisation of large data.
Insert > PivotTable. Four field zones: Rows, Columns, Values, Filters.
Value Field Settings: Sum / Count / Average / Max / Min / Product.
Subtotal (Data > Subtotal) inserts =SUBTOTAL() formulas after sorting.
Pivot Table is the modern answer; Subtotal is the legacy answer.
tricks: If the option lists 'Pivot Table' for 'summarise large data' -> right.
If the option lists 'a formula you write manually' for the same question -> wrong (that's a regular formula, not the summarisation tool).
Pivot Table needs a header row in the source data - 'My data has headers' must be true (it is by default).
patterns: 'Which tool summarises large data with drag-and-drop?' -> Pivot Table.
'Where do the four field zones (Rows, Columns, Values, Filters) live?' -> PivotTable Fields pane on the right.
'To change Sum to Count in a pivot value?' -> Right-click > Value Field Settings.

formulas.title: Cell Reference Types (Relative / Absolute / Mixed)

formula.text: No $ = relative (shifts on copy). $A$1 = absolute (locked on both). $A1 = column locked, row relative. A$1 = row locked, column relative.

formulas.whenToUse: Any 'what does $ mean in a cell reference?' or 'how to keep a value constant when copying a formula?' MCQ. Also 'which F4 cycle?' questions.
explanation: RELATIVE reference (A1): default. When you copy the formula down a column, the row number increments. =A1*2 in B1, copied to B2, becomes =A2*2.
ABSOLUTE reference ($A$1): row AND column are locked. The reference does NOT change when you copy. =$A$1*2 in B1, copied to B2, stays =$A$1*2.

MIXED - column locked (the column letter has the dollar sign): the column letter is locked but the row number still changes. =A1*2 in B1 with the column part locked, copied to B2, becomes a row-shifted reference.

MIXED - row locked (the row number has the dollar sign): the row number is locked but the column letter still changes. =A1*2 in B1 with the row part locked, copied to C1, becomes a column-shifted reference.
F4 cycles through the four states: A1 -> absolute -> row-locked -> column-locked -> back to A1.
Practical use: absolute for tax rates or fixed multipliers; mixed for lookup tables with one locked row or column.

example.prompt: You have a tax rate in $A$1. You want every cell in B to show A*tax. The formula in B1 is:
steps: Tax rate must not change when you copy down - it is in $A$1.
Column A reference should change to A1, A2, A3 - relative.

formulas.memoryTip: A dollar sign locks whatever it is in front of. Dollar-A locks the column. A-dollar locks the row. Dollar-A-dollar-1 locks both.
formulas.commonMistake: Forgetting the dollar before the row when you want the row to stay fixed (A-dollar-1, not A1).

formulas.title: VLOOKUP Anatomy (and the FALSE trap)

formula.text: =VLOOKUP(what, where, which column, exact or approximate). FALSE = exact. TRUE/omitted = approximate (needs sorted data).

formulas.whenToUse: Any VLOOKUP / HLOOKUP / lookup-function MCQ. The FALSE/TRUE distinction is the most-asked trap.
explanation: lookup_value: the value to find. Usually a cell reference like A2.
table_array: the range to search in. The lookup column must be the FIRST column of this range. Use absolute references ($A$2:$D$100) so the table doesn't shift when copied.
col_index_num: which column of the table to return. 1 = first column (the lookup column itself), 2 = second column, etc.

range_lookup: FALSE = exact match (always use this in exams and most real work). TRUE or omitted = approximate match (requires the lookup column to be sorted ascending - returns wrong results otherwise).

HLOOKUP is the horizontal version: looks in the first ROW, returns a value from a row below. INDEX-MATCH is more flexible than VLOOKUP: MATCH finds the position, INDEX returns the value. INDEX-MATCH can look LEFT (VLOOKUP cannot).

steps: Find 101 in the FIRST column of A2:D20.
Return the value in the 3rd column of the same row.
FALSE = exact match (so 101 must be present, else #N/A).
example.answer: The value in the 3rd column of the row where the first column equals 101 (exact match).

formulas.memoryTip: VLOOKUP = Vertical LOOKUP. HLOOKUP = Horizontal LOOKUP. The 'V' and 'H' tell you which direction the lookup goes.
formulas.commonMistake: Using TRUE / omitting range_lookup in a non-sorted table - silently returns wrong answers.

formulas.title: Basic Statistical Functions

formula.text: SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, COUNTA, MIN, MAX, MEDIAN. COUNT counts numbers only; COUNTA counts anything non-empty.

formulas.whenToUse: Any 'which function for X?' MCQ where X is a summary statistic.
explanation: SUM(range) - adds all numbers in the range. Empty cells and text are ignored.
AVERAGE(range) - mean. Same ignoring rule as SUM.
COUNT(range) - counts cells containing NUMBERS. Text cells are skipped.
COUNTA(range) - counts cells that are NOT EMPTY, including text and numbers. (A is for 'All'.)
COUNTBLANK(range) - counts empty cells.
MIN(range) / MAX(range) - smallest / largest number. Ignores text and empty.
MEDIAN(range) - middle value when sorted. MODE(range) - most frequent value.
The IF family: SUMIF(range, criteria, sum_range) sums cells meeting a criterion. =SUMIF(B:B, '>100') sums column B values > 100. =COUNTIF(A:A, 'Delhi') counts 'Delhi' in column A.

example.prompt: How many cells in A1:A10 contain numbers?
steps: Use COUNT - it counts numbers only.
=COUNT(A1:A10) returns the count of numeric cells.

formulas.memoryTip: COUNT = numbers. COUNTA = All non-empty. COUNTBLANK = empty. Easy to remember if you imagine COUNT counting only 'real' data.
formulas.commonMistake: Using COUNT when you want to count text (use COUNTA). Using AVERAGE on a range that contains text - it skips text and may give an unexpected mean.

formulas.title: IF, AND, OR, IFERROR

formula.text: IF returns one value or another based on a condition. AND/OR combine conditions. IFERROR replaces error values with a friendly message.

formulas.whenToUse: Any logical-function MCQ. Also used to wrap formulas that may produce #N/A or #DIV/0! so the cell shows a clean message instead.
explanation: IF(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false). Example: =IF(A1>=50, 'Pass', 'Fail').
AND(condition1, condition2, ...) - TRUE only if ALL conditions are true. OR - TRUE if ANY condition is true. NOT(condition) - inverts TRUE/FALSE.
Nested IF: =IF(A1>=90, 'A', IF(A1>=75, 'B', IF(A1>=50, 'C', 'F'))) - chains multiple IFs.

IFERROR(value, value_if_error): if the value expression produces an error (#DIV/0!, #N/A, #VALUE!, #REF!, #NAME?, #NUM!), return value_if_error instead. Example: =IFERROR(VLOOKUP(...), 'Not found') - shows 'Not found' instead of #N/A.

example.prompt: If VLOOKUP doesn't find the value, the cell shows #N/A. How do you show 'Not found' instead?

formulas.memoryTip: IF = 'is this true? then A, else B'. IFERROR = 'did this error? then this, else whatever'.
formulas.commonMistake: Confusing AND and OR. AND wants EVERY condition true; OR wants AT LEAST ONE.

reference-types.q: A cell reference with no $ sign (e.g. A1) is called:
s: No $ = Relative. Reference shifts on copy.
$A$1 = Absolute. $A1 or A$1 = Mixed.

reference-types.q: An absolute reference has $ signs on:
s: $A$1 = absolute: $ before column AND $ before row.
$A1 or A$1 = mixed.

reference-types.q: Shortcut to toggle cell reference types in formula edit mode:
s: Works only when you're inside a formula.

reference-types.q: If =A1 is in cell B1, what does it become when copied to B2?
s: Relative reference: row shifts from 1 to 2 when copied down.
Column doesn't shift (A is still A since B1 to B2 only moved down).

reference-types.q: If =$A$1 is in cell B1, what does it become when copied to B2?
s: Absolute reference: row AND column both locked. Stays $A$1.

reference-types.q: If =A$1 is in cell B1, what does it become when copied to C1?
s: Mixed: row locked ($1), column relative (A -> B).

reference-types.q: Maximum number of rows in an Excel worksheet:
s: Since Excel 2007, max rows = 2^20 = 1,048,576.
Older Excel 2003 had 65,536 rows.

reference-types.q: Maximum number of columns in an Excel worksheet:
s: Since Excel 2007, max columns = 2^14 = 16,384 (XFD).

reference-types.q: Last column letter in modern Excel:
s: The 16,384th column is XFD.
Older Excel 2003 ended at IV.

opts: The last used cell in the worksheet
The last cell of column A
s: Ctrl+End jumps to the last USED cell (the bottom-right corner of your data).
reference-types.a: The last used cell in the worksheet

vlookup-form.q: VLOOKUP looks for the lookup value in which column of the table?
s: VLOOKUP always searches the FIRST column of the table_array.
To look in another column, use INDEX-MATCH.

vlookup-form.q: What does FALSE in VLOOKUP's last argument mean?
s: FALSE = exact match. Use this in exams and most real work.
TRUE/omitted = approximate (needs sorted data).

vlookup-form.q: HLOOKUP looks for the lookup value in the:
s: HLOOKUP = Horizontal LOOKUP. Searches the first ROW and returns from a row below.

opts: Lookup value not found and FALSE used
s: With FALSE (exact), no match -> #N/A. Wrap in IFERROR to show a friendly message.
vlookup-form.a: Lookup value not found and FALSE used

vlookup-form.q: Which combination can look LEFT (return a value to the left of the lookup column)?
s: INDEX-MATCH is the flexible combo. MATCH finds the position, INDEX returns the value.
VLOOKUP can only look right.
col_index_num is the column number within the table (1 = first column = B, 2 = C, 3 = D).

vlookup-form.q: If VLOOKUP's column index is greater than the number of columns in the table:
s: col_index out of range -> #REF! error.
Approximate match uses binary search - the first column must be sorted ascending.
Otherwise it returns wrong answers.

opts: The position of the value in the range
The row number of the cell
s: MATCH returns the position (1, 2, 3, ...) of the value within the range, not the value itself.
vlookup-form.a: The position of the value in the range

opts: In any direction (left, right, up, down)
s: XLOOKUP is the modern replacement for VLOOKUP - looks in any direction.
vlookup-form.a: In any direction (left, right, up, down)

opts: The sum of all numbers in A1:A10
The count of numbers in A1:A10
s: SUM adds all numbers in the range. Text and empty cells are ignored.
stat-functions.a: The sum of all numbers in A1:A10

COUNTA counts all non-empty cells.

opts: Arithmetic mean of numbers in A1:A5
s: AVERAGE = arithmetic mean (sum / count). Skips text.

Use SUMIF to sum a related column.
SUMIF(range to test, criterion, range to sum). Sums C where B > 100.
MAX returns the largest value in the range.
MIN returns the smallest value.
MEDIAN = middle value when the numbers are sorted.

stat-functions.q: Which function counts cells meeting a condition?
s: COUNTIF counts cells meeting a single criterion.
SUMIF sums; AVERAGEIF averages; COUNTIFS is the multi-criteria version.
=IF(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false). >= means 50 OR MORE.

if-and-error.q: =IFERROR(VLOOKUP(A2, range, 3, FALSE), 'Not found') shows 'Not found' when:
s: IFERROR catches errors (#N/A from no match, #REF! from bad column index, #DIV/0!, #VALUE!, etc.) and returns the fallback.

opts: BOTH A1>10 AND B1<100 are true
s: AND returns TRUE only if ALL conditions are true. OR returns TRUE if ANY is true.
if-and-error.a: BOTH A1>10 AND B1<100 are true

s: OR = 'at least one'. AND = 'all'.
if-and-error.a: AT LEAST ONE condition is true

s: First condition checked: A1 >= 90 returns 'A'. Otherwise check next.

if-and-error.q: IFERROR catches which of the following errors?
s: IFERROR catches all six major Excel error values.
NOT inverts the boolean. NOT(TRUE) = FALSE; NOT(FALSE) = TRUE.

if-and-error.q: The IF function's three arguments are:
s: =IF(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false).

if-and-error.q: Which is the right pattern for VLOOKUP-protected-against-N/A?
s: Wrap VLOOKUP in IFERROR to show a friendly message instead of #N/A.

if-and-error.q: What does =IF(A1='Mumbai', 'West', IF(A1='Chennai', 'South', 'Other')) return for A1='Pune'?
s: Neither 'Mumbai' nor 'Chennai' - falls through both IFs to the final 'Other'.

mcqs.q: MS Excel is primarily used for:
exp: Excel is a spreadsheet program - rows, columns, formulas, charts.

mcqs.q: Default file extension of MS Excel 2016+:
exp: .xlsx since Excel 2007. .xls was the pre-2007 extension.
.xlsm is the macro-enabled extension.

mcqs.q: Maximum rows in a modern Excel worksheet:
exp: 2^20 = 1,048,576 rows since Excel 2007.

mcqs.q: Maximum columns in a modern Excel worksheet:
exp: 2^14 = 16,384 columns (XFD) since Excel 2007.

mcqs.q: Last column letter in modern Excel:
exp: The 16,384th column is XFD.
Older Excel 2003 ended at IV (256 columns).

mcqs.q: Shortcut to toggle between relative and absolute references:
exp: F4 cycles A1 -> $A$1 -> A$1 -> $A1 -> A1 (in formula edit mode).

mcqs.q: A cell reference with $ before both column letter and row number ($A$1) is:
exp: $A$1 = absolute: both column and row are locked.

mcqs.q: If =A1 is in B1 and you copy it to B2, the formula becomes:
exp: Relative reference: row shifts from 1 to 2 when copied down.

mcqs.q: VLOOKUP looks for the lookup value in the:
exp: VLOOKUP always searches the FIRST column of the table_array.

mcqs.q: What does FALSE in VLOOKUP's last argument mean?
exp: FALSE = exact match. Use this in exams and most real work.

mcqs.q: HLOOKUP looks for the lookup value in the:
exp: HLOOKUP = Horizontal. Searches the first ROW, returns from a row below.

mcqs.q: Which combination can look LEFT (return a value to the left of the lookup column)?
exp: INDEX-MATCH: MATCH finds the position, INDEX returns the value. Can look any direction.

mcqs.q: =SUM(A1:A10) returns:
opts: The sum of all numbers in A1:A10
exp: SUM adds all numbers in the range. Text and empty cells are ignored.

mcqs.q: =COUNT(A1:A10) counts:
exp: COUNT counts cells containing NUMBERS only.

mcqs.q: =COUNTA(A1:A10) counts:
exp: COUNTA = 'Count All' non-empty. Includes text and numbers.

mcqs.q: =AVERAGE(A1:A5) returns:
exp: AVERAGE = arithmetic mean (sum / count of numeric cells).

mcqs.q: =COUNTIF(A:A, 'Delhi') returns:
exp: COUNTIF counts cells matching the single criterion.

mcqs.q: =SUMIF(B:B, '>100', C:C) returns:
exp: SUMIF(test range, criterion, sum range) - sums C where B meets the criterion.

mcqs.q: =MAX(A1:A10) returns:
exp: MAX = largest value in the range.

mcqs.q: =MIN(A1:A10) returns:
exp: MIN = smallest value.

mcqs.q: =IF(A1>=50, 'Pass', 'Fail') returns 'Pass' when:
exp: IF(condition, true_val, false_val). >= means 50 or more.

mcqs.q: =IFERROR(VLOOKUP(...), 'Not found') catches:
exp: IFERROR catches all six error types: #N/A, #REF!, #DIV/0!, #VALUE!, #NAME?, #NUM!.

mcqs.q: AND(A1>10, B1<100) returns TRUE when:
opts: BOTH A1>10 AND B1<100 are true
exp: AND = ALL conditions true. OR = ANY condition true.

mcqs.q: OR(A1>10, B1<100) returns TRUE when:
exp: OR = 'at least one'.

mcqs.q: Shortcut to go to cell A1:
exp: Ctrl+Home jumps to A1.

mcqs.q: Shortcut to jump to the last used cell:
exp: Ctrl+End = last USED cell (bottom-right of the data).

mcqs.q: Shortcut to open Go To dialog:
exp: F5 opens Go To. (Ctrl+G also works in older Excel; the canonical shortcut is F5.)

mcqs.q: Shortcut to switch to the next worksheet:
exp: Ctrl+Page Down / Ctrl+Page Up move between worksheet tabs.

mcqs.q: Shortcut to insert a new worksheet:
exp: Shift+F11 inserts a new worksheet. F11 creates a default chart.

mcqs.q: Shortcut to open the Format Cells dialog:
exp: Ctrl+1 opens the Format Cells dialog with all number / font / alignment / border options.

mcqs.q: A cell contains 0.85 and is formatted as Percentage. The cell displays:
exp: Percentage format multiplies by 100 and adds %. 0.85 -> 85%.

mcqs.q: Shortcut to create a default column chart on a new sheet:
exp: F11 creates a default chart on a new sheet ('Chart1'). Alt+F1 puts it on the same sheet.

mcqs.q: Which chart type is best for showing trends over time?
exp: Line charts are the standard for showing a trend over time.

mcqs.q: Which chart type is best for showing proportions of a whole?
exp: Pie charts show parts of a whole (percentages summing to 100%).

mcqs.q: Which chart type shows the relationship between two numeric variables?
exp: Scatter (X-Y) plots show correlation between two numeric variables.

mcqs.q: Where do you find the Sort and Filter commands in Excel?
exp: Data tab owns Sort, Filter, Remove Duplicates, Text to Columns, Subtotal.

mcqs.q: Which shortcut opens Find in Excel?
exp: Ctrl+F = Find. Ctrl+H = Replace. F5 = Go To.

mcqs.q: Which shortcut opens Find and Replace in Excel?
exp: Ctrl+H opens the Replace dialog.

mcqs.q: To split a column of full names into first and last name columns, use:
exp: Text to Columns splits a column using a delimiter (comma, space, tab) or fixed width.

mcqs.q: To highlight duplicate values without deleting them:
exp: Conditional Formatting > Highlight Cells Rules > Duplicate Values highlights without deleting.

mcqs.q: Data > Remove Duplicates does what?
opts: Permanently deletes rows with repeated values
Sorts unique values to the top
exp: Remove Duplicates is DESTRUCTIVE - it deletes the duplicate rows. (It asks to confirm first.)

mcqs.q: Best tool to summarise a large flat dataset (e.g. sales per region per product):
exp: Pivot Table = drag-and-drop summarisation of large data with categories and aggregates.

mcqs.q: In a Pivot Table, the four field zones are:
exp: PivotTable Fields pane: Rows (categories down), Columns (categories across), Values (numbers to aggregate), Filters (a top-level filter).

mcqs.q: To change Sum to Count in a Pivot Table value:
opts: Use a different function in the Values box
exp: Right-click any value in the pivot -> Value Field Settings -> choose Count (or Average, Max, Min, etc.).

mcqs.q: Data > Subtotal inserts which formulas?
exp: Subtotal inserts =SUBTOTAL() formulas below each group after you sort by the same column.

mcqs.q: A1 contains 0.85 formatted as Percentage. The formula bar shows:
exp: The formula bar shows the underlying VALUE (0.85). The cell DISPLAYS 85%. Format only changes display.

mcqs.q: What does =AVERAGE(A1:A5) return if A1:A5 contains one text cell and four numbers?
opts: Average of the four numbers (text is skipped)
The text value as a number
exp: AVERAGE skips text and empty cells - it averages only the four numbers.

mcqs.q: Which function returns the position of a value in a range?
exp: MATCH returns the position (1, 2, 3, ...) of the value within the range.

mcqs.q: =INDEX(A2:D10, 5, 2) returns:
opts: The value in the 5th column and 2nd row of A2:D10
The value in the 2nd column and 5th row of A2:D10
exp: INDEX(array, row_num, column_num). Row 5, column 2 of the 9-row x 4-column range.

mcqs.q: VLOOKUP returns #N/A when:
opts: The lookup value is not found with FALSE
exp: With exact match (FALSE), no match found -> #N/A. Wrap in IFERROR to clean up.

mcqs.q: The Name Box in Excel shows:
opts: The formula in the active cell
The address of the active cell
exp: The Name Box (left of the formula bar) shows the address (A1, B5, XFD1048576) of the active cell.

mcqs.q: To freeze the top row so it stays visible when scrolling, use:
opts: View > Freeze Panes > Freeze Top Row
exp: View > Freeze Panes > Freeze Top Row keeps row 1 visible.

mcqs.q: Ctrl+Page Down in Excel moves to:
exp: Ctrl+Page Down / Ctrl+Page Up move between worksheet tabs.

mcqs.q: An Excel workbook contains:
exp: A workbook = the .xlsx file. It contains one or more worksheets (the tabs at the bottom).

mcqs.q: In VLOOKUP, the table_array must have the lookup column as the:
exp: VLOOKUP searches the FIRST column of the table_array by design.

mcqs.q: To remove duplicate rows permanently from a dataset, use:
exp: Data > Remove Duplicates deletes rows. Conditional Formatting only highlights.

mcqs.q: Excel's 'Tell me what you want to do' box is used to:
opts: Search for any command by name
exp: The 'Tell me' / 'Search' box finds any command by name.

mcqs.q: How do you rename a worksheet tab?
exp: Both right-click > Rename AND Home > Format > Rename Sheet work. Or just double-click the tab.

mcqs.q: The default file extension for a macro-enabled Excel workbook is:
exp: .xlsm = Excel with macros enabled.
.xlsx = without macros.
.xlsb = binary format (also macro-enabled).

mcqs.q: A Pivot Table's VALUES zone aggregates numbers by default using:
exp: By default, dragging a numeric field to Values uses Sum. Right-click > Value Field Settings to change.
